sentences.t:
Ðā wæs gegongen guman unfrōdum
earfoðlīce, þæt hē on eorðan geseah
þone lēofestan līfes æt ende
blēate gebǣran.
sentences.l: Then it had come about, hard-wise, for the unwise man, that he saw on the earth the dearest one at life’s end bear himself wretchedly.
sentences.i: It went hard then with the young and untried man, when he saw on the ground the one he loved best, at the end of his life, lying in a sorry state.
sentences.n: ‘Wæs gegongen’ is an impersonal passive of ‘gegān’ (‘go, come about, befall’): ‘it had come about’, with the person it befell in the dative (‘guman unfrōdum’) and the thing that befell in a ‘þæt’-clause (‘þæt hē … geseah’, ‘that he saw’). ‘earfoðlīce’ is an adverb, ‘with hardship, grievously’. ‘Geseah’ takes an accusative (‘þone lēofestan’, ‘the dearest one’, superlative of ‘lēof’, Beowulf) and an infinitive, ‘gebǣran’ (‘behave, bear oneself’), so ‘saw him bear himself wretchedly’, with ‘blēate’ (‘wretchedly’) as the adverb; the sense is that he saw him lying in misery. ‘līfes æt ende’ is ‘at life’s end’. ‘unfrōd’ is ‘not wise’, here ‘inexperienced, young’, and the word is chosen against the ‘frōd’ (‘old and wise’) Beowulf. The ‘an’ of ‘guman’ is in italic: the manuscript has ‘gumū’, which is ‘gumum’, a plural (‘for unwise men’); Heyne changed it to the singular ‘guman’, and Klaeber follows, since the one man is Wīglāf. Klaeber puts no canto number here, but the capital ‘Ð’ of ‘Ðā’ begins a new line in the manuscript, which is why we start the fitt at this line.

sentences.t:
Bona swylce læg,
egeslīc eorðdraca ealdre berēafod,
bealwe gebǣded.
sentences.l: The slayer lay likewise, the dreadful earth-dragon, robbed of life, pressed by bale.
sentences.i: The slayer lay there too, the dreadful earth-dragon, robbed of life and brought down by his hurt.
sentences.n: ‘Bona’ is ‘slayer’, the dragon, who was himself the slayer of Beowulf; ‘swylce’ is ‘likewise’ and joins his lying dead to Beowulf’s. ‘Egeslīc eorðdraca’ is ‘dreadful earth-dragon’ (the house word for ‘eorðdraca’; the dragon lives in the earth-hall). ‘Ealdre berēafod’ is ‘robbed of life’: ‘berēafod’ is the past participle of ‘berēafian’ (‘rob, deprive’), and ‘ealdre’ (from ‘ealdor’, ‘life’) a dative. ‘Bealwe gebǣded’ is ‘pressed by bale’: ‘gebǣded’ is the participle of ‘gebǣdan’ (‘force, oppress’) and ‘bealwe’ a dative of ‘bealu’ (‘evil, harm’); I take it to mean that the dragon is overcome by the harm done him, and the exact force of ‘gebǣded’ is a little uncertain.

sentences.t:
Bēahhordum leng
wyrm wōhbogen wealdan ne mōste,
ac him īrenna ecga fornāmon,
hearde heaðoscearde homera lāfe,
þæt se wīdfloga wundum stille
hrēas on hrūsan hordærne nēah.
sentences.l: Of ring-hoards longer the worm, crooked-bowed, might not be ruler, but iron edges took him off, hard, battle-notched, the leavings of hammers, so that the wide-flier, still with wounds, fell on the ground near the hoard-house.
sentences.i: The dragon, coiled and crooked, could be master of the ring-hoards no longer; but the iron edges had taken him off, hard blades notched in battle, what the hammers left, so that the far-flier, stilled by his wounds, fell upon the ground near the hoard-house.
sentences.n: ‘Wealdan’ takes the dative (‘bēahhordum’, ‘ring-hoards’), and ‘ne mōste’ is ‘might not, was not allowed’, with ‘leng’ (‘longer’): the dragon was no longer allowed to rule his hoard. The house word ‘wyrm’ is ‘worm’ in ‘l’ and ‘dragon’ in ‘i’. ‘Wōhbogen’ is ‘crooked-bowed’ (‘wōh’ ‘crooked’ + ‘bogen’, ‘bent’), the dragon’s curled, bent body. ‘ac him īrenna ecga fornāmon’: ‘ecga’ is the plural subject, ‘edges’, ‘īrenna’ depends on it (‘of irons’, that is, of swords), and ‘fornāmon’ (‘fornīman’, ‘take away, destroy’) has the dragon as its object; Klaeber prints ‘him’, a dative of the one affected (‘took off from him’), and ‘l’ and ‘i’ render it as ‘took him off’; Grein (with a query), Rieger and others read ‘hine’, an accusative, the object this verb normally takes. ‘Hearde heaðoscearde homera lāfe’ is a string of words in apposition to ‘ecga’: ‘hard, battle-notched (‘heaðo’ + ‘sceard’, ‘notched, hacked’), the leavings of hammers’, the blades being what the hammers left when they had finished forging them; Thorpe and others read ‘-scearpe’, ‘battle-sharp’. ‘Þæt se wīdfloga … hrēas’ is a result clause, ‘so that the wide-flier fell’, with ‘wundum stille’ ‘still with wounds’, a dative of cause; ‘hordærn’ is the house ‘hoard-house’.

sentences.t:
Nalles æfter lyfte lācende hwearf
middelnihtum, māðmæhta wlonc
ansȳn ȳwde, ac hē eorðan gefēoll
for ðæs hildfruman hondgeweorce.
sentences.l: Not at all along the air, playing, did he go to and fro at midnights, proud of his treasure-possessions, show his face, but he fell to earth because of the battle-leader’s hand-work.
sentences.i: He did not go sweeping through the air at midnight, playing on the wing and proud of his treasure, nor show himself; he fell to the earth instead, brought down by the battle-leader’s handiwork.
sentences.n: ‘Nalles’ is ‘not at all’, and the sentence turns on it: ‘nalles … hwearf … ac hē … gefēoll’, ‘he did not wheel … but he fell’. ‘Æfter lyfte’ is ‘along the air’ (‘æfter’ with the dative means ‘along, through’), ‘lācende’ is a present participle, ‘playing’ (‘lācan’ can mean ‘play’ and also ‘fly, fight’), and ‘middelnihtum’ is a dative plural of time, ‘at midnights’. ‘Māðmæhta wlonc’ is ‘proud of treasure-possessions’, the genitive plural after ‘wlonc’ (‘proud’). ‘Ansȳn ȳwde’ is ‘showed his face’, that is, appeared (‘ȳwan’ ‘show’). ‘Eorðan’ is ‘to earth’ (the weak feminine ending serves for dative and accusative alike), ‘for ðæs hildfruman hondgeweorce’ is ‘because of the battle-leader’s hand-work’ (‘hild’ ‘battle’ + ‘fruma’ ‘first one, leader’), the battle-leader being Beowulf, and ‘hondgeweorc’ his handiwork, the wound he gave the dragon.

sentences.t:
Hūru þæt on lande lȳt manna ðāh
mægenāgendra mīne gefrǣge,
þēah ðe hē dǣda gehwæs dyrstig wǣre,
þæt hē wið attorsceaðan oreðe gerǣsde,
oððe hringsele hondum styrede,
gif hē wæccende weard onfunde
būon on beorge.
sentences.l: Indeed, in this few of men in the land throve, of the power-possessing, by my hearsay, though he were bold in every deed, that he should rush against the poison-scather’s breath, or stir the ring-hall with hands, if he found a waking guardian dwelling on the barrow.
sentences.i: Few men in the land, mighty as they were, have prospered at this, as I have heard, however bold in every deed: to rush against the poison-scather’s breath, or lay hands on the ring-hall, if they found its guardian awake and dwelling on the barrow.
sentences.n: This is a hard sentence to take apart, and the order of the Old English is kept in ‘l’. The first ‘þæt’ looks forward to the second: ‘ðāh’ (past of ‘þēon’, ‘thrive, succeed’) is ‘few of men throve in this, that he …’, with the second ‘þæt hē … gerǣsde … oððe … styrede’ naming what no one thrived at; I take the first ‘þæt’ as that anticipating word, and the construction is a guess. ‘Lȳt manna’ is ‘few of men’ (partitive genitive) with ‘mægenāgendra’ (‘of those who possess strength’) beside it, and ‘mīne gefrǣge’ is ‘by my hearsay’, the poet’s ‘as I have heard’. ‘Þēah ðe hē … wǣre’ is ‘though he were’, subjunctive, and ‘dyrstig’ (‘bold’) takes the genitive ‘dǣda gehwæs’ (‘in every deed’). ‘Gerǣsde’ and ‘styrede’ are subjunctives too, ‘should rush’, ‘should stir’: ‘gerǣsan wið’ is ‘rush against’, ‘oreðe’ is ‘breath’ (the fire-breath), and ‘attorsceaðan’ is ‘poison-scather’ (‘ator’ ‘poison’ + ‘sceaða’ ‘scather, harmer’; compare the house ‘ūhtsceaða’). ‘Hringsele’ is ‘ring-hall’, the treasure-house. ‘Gif hē wæccende weard onfunde būon on beorge’ is ‘if he found a waking guardian dwelling on the barrow’, with ‘wæccende’ (‘waking’) and the infinitive ‘būon’ (‘dwell’) after ‘onfunde’. The point is that no man, however brave, had the better of a dragon that was on guard; Beowulf did it only at the cost of his life.

sentences.t:
Bīowulfe wearð
dryhtmāðma dǣl dēaðe forgolden;
sentences.l: To Beowulf the share of lord-treasures was paid for with death;
sentences.i: Beowulf’s share of the noble treasures was paid for with death;
sentences.n: ‘Wearð … forgolden’ is a passive of ‘forgyldan’ (‘pay for, repay’), ‘was paid for’, with the dative ‘dēaðe’ (‘with death’) saying what the price was, and ‘Bīowulfe’ is the dative ‘to / for Beowulf’. ‘Dryhtmāðma dǣl’ is ‘the share of lord-treasures’ (a genitive plural depending on ‘dǣl’). ‘Dryht-’ is a word for a troop or retinue, and the compound occurs only here in the poem; ‘l’ ‘lord-treasures’ keeps the literal sense (treasures of the lord’s company), and ‘i’ ‘noble treasures’ rests on the sense ‘noble, lordly’ that ‘dryht-’ has in other compounds such as ‘dryhtlīc’. Both are guesses. What Beowulf got from the hoard, then, he bought with his life.

sentences.t:
hæfde ǣghwæðer ende gefēred
lǣnan līfes.
sentences.l: Each of the two had accomplished the end of lent life.
sentences.i: Each of the two had come to the end of a life that was only lent.
sentences.n: ‘Hæfde … gefēred’ is the plain past perfect (‘had brought to an end’), with ‘ende’ as object and ‘lǣnan līfes’ (‘of lent life’, genitive) depending on it; ‘gefēran’ is ‘bring about, accomplish’. ‘ǣghwæðer’ is ‘each of two’ and the verb is singular, so ‘each had …’. The ‘er’ of ‘ǣghwæðer’ is in italic because the manuscript has ‘æghwæðre’, which Kemble (in his second edition) altered to the nominative ‘ǣghwæðer’, and Klaeber follows. The two are Beowulf and the dragon. ‘Lǣne’ means ‘lent, on loan’, the same idea as the house ‘lǣndagas’ (‘lent days’): life is a loan to be repaid.

sentences.t:
Næs ðā lang tō ðon,
þæt ðā hildlatan holt ofgēfan,
tȳdre trēowlogan tȳne ætsomne,
ðā ne dorston ǣr dareðum lācan
on hyra mandryhtnes miclan þearfe;
sentences.l: It was not long then until the battle-laggards left the wood, the timid troth-breakers, ten together, they who before had not dared to play with darts in their liege-lord’s great need;
sentences.i: It was not long before the slackers in battle left the wood, ten cowardly oath-breakers together, who earlier had not dared to ply their darts in their liege-lord’s great need;
sentences.n: ‘Næs ðā lang tō ðon, þæt …’ is ‘it was not long to that (point) that …’, a fixed way of saying ‘it was not long before’. The subject is ‘hildlatan’ (‘battle-laggards’, ‘hild’ ‘battle’ + ‘lata’ ‘slow one’), named in three appositions: ‘tȳdre’ (‘timid, weak’), ‘trēowlogan’ (‘troth-breakers’, ‘trēow’ ‘faith’ + ‘loga’, from the root of ‘lie’), and ‘tȳne’ (‘ten’) ‘ætsomne’ (‘together’). These are the ten who ran into the wood when the dragon came out (earlier in the poem). ‘Ofgēfan’ is the plural past of ‘ofgifan’, ‘give up, leave’. ‘Ðā ne dorston’ is ‘they who dared not’ (‘dorston’, past of ‘durran’), and ‘dareðum lācan’ is ‘play with darts’, ‘lācan’ taking the dative of the weapons: a gentle word for fighting. ‘Mandryhtnes’ is the genitive of the house ‘mandryhten’ (‘liege-lord’), here Beowulf.

sentences.t:
ac hȳ scamiende scyldas bǣran,
gūðgewǣdu þǣr se gomela læg;
sentences.l: but they, ashamed, bore their shields, their war-garments, there where the old one lay;
sentences.i: but ashamed they carried their shields and war-gear to the place where the old man lay;
sentences.n: ‘Ac hȳ scamiende scyldas bǣran’: ‘scamiende’ is a present participle, ‘being ashamed’, ‘bǣran’ is the plural past of ‘beran’ (‘bore’; Klaeber’s ending is ‘-an’ for ‘-on’), and ‘scyldas’ and ‘gūðgewǣdu’ (‘war-garments’, accusative plural) are its objects. ‘Þǣr’ is ‘where’; with a verb of carrying, ‘i’ takes it as ‘to the place where’, supplying the coming-up that the verb does not itself say. ‘Se gomela’ is ‘the old one’, Beowulf.

sentences.t: wlitan on Wīlāf.
sentences.l: they looked on Wīlāf.
sentences.i: and looked at Wīlāf.
sentences.n: ‘Wlitan’ is the plural past of ‘wlītan’ (‘look’), with ‘on’ and the accusative, ‘looked at’, so it continues the sentence of the unit before: they came with shields and gear, ashamed, and looked at Wiglaf. Klaeber prints the short ‘i’; Kemble, Sievers and others print ‘wlītan’, an infinitive, ‘to look’, which would read as part of what they did in coming. ‘Wīlāf’ is the same name as Wīglāf with the ‘g’ lost (Klaeber prints both).

sentences.l: He sat wearied, the foot-fighter, near the lord’s shoulders, he roused him with water;
sentences.i: He sat there weary, the foot-fighter, close by his lord’s shoulders, and tried to rouse him with water;
sentences.n: ‘Gewērgad’ is a past participle, ‘wearied’, used as an adjective with ‘sæt’. ‘Fēðecempa’ is ‘foot-fighter’ (house word; ‘fēþe’ ‘on foot’ + ‘cempa’ ‘warrior’) in apposition to ‘hē’, that is, Wīglāf. ‘Frēan eaxlum nēah’ is ‘near the lord’s shoulders’: ‘nēah’ takes the dative, ‘eaxlum’ is dative plural, and ‘frēan’ is the genitive of ‘frēa’, ‘lord’. ‘Wehte hyne wætre’ is ‘roused him with water’, ‘wehte’ being the past of ‘weccan’ (‘rouse, wake’; the past of ‘wecgan’, ‘shake’, would be ‘wegde’) and ‘wætre’ the dative of the means; he is trying to bring Beowulf round, as he did in the last fitt.

sentences.t: him wiht ne spēow.
sentences.l: to him it did not at all succeed.
sentences.i: it did him no good at all.
sentences.n: ‘Spēow’ is the past of ‘spōwan’, ‘succeed, prosper’, used without a subject (‘it succeeded’), with the person in the dative (‘him’), and ‘wiht ne’ is the strong negative, ‘not at all’. The ‘w’ of ‘spēow’ is in italic: the manuscript has ‘speop’, and Thorkelin printed ‘spēow’. The Old English ‘p’ and the runic letter ‘wynn’ (‘ƿ’), which stands for ‘w’, look alike in the script, a possible cause of the copying slip.

sentences.l: He could not on earth, though he wished it well, keep life in the chieftain, nor turn anything of the Wielder’s aside;
sentences.i: However much he wished it, he could not keep the life in his chief on earth, nor turn aside anything that the Wielder willed;
sentences.n: ‘Ne meahte hē … feorh gehealdan’ is ‘he could not keep life’, with the infinitive ‘gehealdan’ and the object ‘feorh’; the subject is Wīglāf, and ‘on ðām frumgāre’ is ‘in the chieftain’ (‘frum-’ ‘first’ + ‘gār’ ‘spear’, so the foremost spear-man, a chief). ‘Ðēah hē ūðe wēl’ is ‘though he wished it well’: ‘ūðe’ is the past of ‘unnan’, ‘grant, wish’, and the same verb is used of God at 2874, where it means ‘granted’. ‘Nē ðæs Wealdendes wiht oncirran’ is ‘nor turn aside anything of the Wielder’s’, ‘oncirran’ being ‘turn, change’ and ‘Wealdend’ (‘Wielder’, house word) God; ‘wiht’ is the object (‘anything’) and ‘ðæs Wealdendes’ a genitive. Thorpe and others read ‘willan’ for ‘wiht’, ‘change the Wielder’s will’, which gives the same sense in plainer words (‘i’ supplies ‘willed’ in that spirit, since ‘anything of the Wielder’s’ is not English), and one scholar reads ‘weorldendes’ (‘the world’s end’?) for ‘Wealdendes’.

sentences.t:
wolde dōm Godes dǣdum rǣdan
gumena gehwylcum, swā hē nū gēn dêð.
sentences.l: The judgment of God would rule in deeds over each of men, as he still does now.
sentences.i: The judgment of God would rule the deeds of every man, as he still does.
sentences.n: ‘Wolde’ is ‘would’, with the infinitive ‘rǣdan’ (‘rule, decide’); the subject is ‘dōm Godes’, ‘God’s judgment’, and ‘dǣdum’ is a dative plural, ‘in deeds’, with ‘gumena gehwylcum’ (‘over each of men’) beside it; the construction is loose and I read it as ‘God’s judgment would decide in the matter of deeds for every man’. Bu. (Bugge) reads ‘dēað ārǣdan’ (‘Death would decree’), which changes the words but not the thought of an unalterable end. ‘Swā hē nū gēn dêð’ is ‘as he still now does’; the circumflex marks that ‘dêð’ is a contracted form of ‘dēþ’ (from ‘dōn’, ‘do’), ‘does’; the subject ‘hē’ is God, or his ‘dōm’ (both are masculine), and ‘l’ and ‘i’ keep the plain ‘he’. The poet speaks here in his own voice, a Christian saying that God’s sentence governs all.

sentences.t:
Þā wæs æt ðām geongan grim andswaru
ēðbegēte þām ðe ǣr his elne forlēas.
sentences.l: Then was from the young man a grim answer easy to obtain for him who before had lost his courage.
sentences.i: Then it was easy for one who had earlier lost his courage to get a grim answer from the young man.
sentences.n: ‘Æt ðām geongan’ is ‘from the young man’, ‘æt’ with the dative meaning ‘from’; ‘wæs … ēðbegēte’ is ‘was easy to get’ (‘ēþe’ ‘easy’ + ‘begēte’ ‘obtainable’), and ‘þām ðe’ is ‘for him who’. ‘His elne forlēas’ is ‘lost his courage’, ‘elne’ is a dative (‘ellen’ has the genitive ‘elnes’, as at 2876) and ‘his’ the possessive. The ‘an’ of ‘geongan’ is in italic: the manuscript has ‘geongū’, a plural, and Barnouw, Holthausen and Schücking altered it to the singular; Lichtenheld doubtfully defended the plural. ‘Grim andswaru’ is a ‘grim answer’, and the one who gets it is the coward (‘þām ðe’). ‘Þām’ is singular, but the group meant is the ten.

sentences.t:
Wīglāf maðelode, Wēohstānes sunu,
sec[g] sārigferð — seah on unlēofe —:
sentences.l: Wīglāf spoke in speech-words, Wēohstān’s son, the man sore of spirit — he looked at the unloved —:
sentences.i: Wīglāf spoke in formal words, the son of Wēohstān, a man heavy at heart — he looked on those he loved not —:
sentences.n: The house formula ‘maðelode’ is ‘spoke in speech-words’ (‘spoke in formal words’ in the idiomatic version); Klaeber spells it with ‘ð’ here and ‘þ’ elsewhere, one word. ‘Wēohstānes sunu’ is ‘Wēohstān’s son’, genitive, in apposition to Wīglāf; Klaeber prints the father’s name ‘Wīhstān’ at 2752 and ‘Wēohstān’ here. ‘Sec[g] sārigferð’ is ‘a man sore of spirit’ (‘sārig’ ‘sore, sad’ + ‘ferhð’ ‘spirit’), another appositive. The ‘g’ in square brackets is a letter Klaeber added: the manuscript has ‘sec’, and Thorkelin supplied the ‘g’, giving ‘secg’, ‘man’. ‘Seah on unlēofe’ is ‘looked at the unloved’, ‘on’ with the accusative, ‘unlēofe’ being those who are not dear to him, the cowards (the adjective used as a noun, plural). The dashes and the colon introduce the speech.

sentences.t: ‘Þæt, lā, mæg secgan sē ðe wyle sōð specan,
sentences.l: ‘That, lo, can say he who will speak the truth,
sentences.i: ‘Lo, this much can be said by anyone who will speak the truth,
sentences.n: ‘Þæt’ is the object of ‘secgan’ and looks forward to the clause that begins on the next line, ‘þæt se mondryhten’, whose verb ‘forwurpe’ comes only at 2871 (a second ‘þæt’ there picks the clause up again after the parenthesis); the sentence is long and interrupted, so ‘l’ keeps ‘that … that’. ‘Lā’ is ‘lo’, an exclamation to rouse attention. ‘Mæg secgan sē ðe wyle sōð specan’ is ‘can say he who will speak truth’, ‘sē ðe’ meaning ‘he who’ and ‘wyle’ ‘wishes to, will’. ‘Sōð specan’ is ‘speak truth’ with ‘sōð’ the noun, ‘truth’.

sentences.t:
þæt se mondryhten, sē ēow ðā māðmas geaf,
ēoredgeatwe, þē gē þǣr on standað, —
sentences.l: that the liege-lord, he who gave you those treasures, the troop-gear in which you stand there, —
sentences.i: that the liege-lord who gave you those treasures, the war-gear in which you stand there, —
sentences.n: ‘Þæt se mondryhten’ begins the clause, with ‘mondryhten’ a spelling of the house ‘mandryhten’ (‘liege-lord’), here Beowulf. ‘Sē ēow ðā māðmas geaf’ is ‘he who gave you those treasures’ with ‘ēow’ a dative plural, ‘to you’, and ‘ēoredgeatwe’ (‘ēored’ ‘troop, cavalry’ + ‘geatwe’ ‘equipment’) in apposition to ‘māðmas’; Klaeber’s dash after ‘standað’ opens a parenthesis that does not close until the end of 2870. ‘Þē gē þǣr on standað’ is ‘in which you there stand’, ‘þē’ being the relative particle (‘which’) and ‘on’ going with ‘standað’, ‘stand in’, so the gear is on their bodies as Wīglāf speaks.

sentences.t:
þonne hē on ealubence oft gesealde
healsittendum helm ond byrnan,
þēoden his þegnum, swylce hē þrȳðlīcost
ōwer feor oððe nēah findan meahte —,
sentences.l: when he often gave on the ale-bench to the hall-sitting ones helmet and byrnie, the prince to his thanes, such as most splendid he could find anywhere, far or near —,
sentences.i: when he often gave helmet and byrnie to his hall-sitters on the ale-bench, the prince to his thanes, the most splendid that he could find anywhere, far or near —
sentences.n: The parenthesis fills in what ‘ēoredgeatwe’ meant: ‘þonne hē … oft gesealde’ is ‘when he often gave’, with ‘ealubence’ (‘ale-bench’) a dative after ‘on’, and the receivers ‘healsittendum’ (‘hall-sitters’, dative plural), with ‘þegnum’ (‘thanes’) in apposition to them, and ‘þēoden’ (‘prince’) in apposition to the subject ‘hē’. Gifts of helmets and mail were given at the feast, where the lord paid his followers. ‘Swylce hē þrȳðlīcost ōwer feor oððe nēah findan meahte’ is ‘such (things) as he, most splendidly, could find anywhere, far or near’: ‘swylce’ is ‘such as’ and ‘þrȳðlīcost’ the superlative of ‘þrȳðlīc’ (‘splendid, mighty’). Klaeber prints ‘þrȳð-’ with the length mark; the manuscript has ‘pryd-’, which Thorkelin and the editors (except Arnold and Chambers) read as ‘þrȳð-’. Trautmann reads ‘ēow’ for ‘oft’ (‘gave to you’).

sentences.t:
þæt hē gēnunga gūðgewǣdu
wrāðe forwurpe, ðā hyne wīg beget.
sentences.l: that he utterly threw away his war-garments, bitterly, when battle befell him.
sentences.i: that he flung away the war-gear utterly and in vain, when war came upon him.
sentences.n: This takes up the clause begun at 2865 (‘þæt se mondryhten’) that ‘Þæt … mæg secgan’ was waiting for: ‘þæt hē … forwurpe’, ‘that he threw away’, a subjunctive (‘forwurpe’, from ‘forweorpan’, ‘cast away’) in a clause of what is said. ‘Gēnunga’ is ‘utterly, wholly’. ‘Wrāðe’ is an adverb of ‘wrāð’ (‘angry, cruel, bitter’); I give ‘bitterly’ in ‘l’ and ‘in vain’ in ‘i’, and that is a guess, since the idea is that the gifts were wasted, thrown away as good as worthless in the hour of need. ‘Ðā hyne wīg beget’ is ‘when battle got him’: ‘beget’ is the past of ‘begietan’, ‘get, befall’.

sentences.t:
Nealles folccyning fyrdgesteallum
gylpan þorfte;
sentences.l: Not at all had the folk-king need to boast of his war-companions;
sentences.i: The king of the people had no cause to boast of his companions in arms;
sentences.n: ‘Nealles’ is ‘not at all’ (the same word as ‘nalles’ in 2832). ‘Gylpan þorfte’ is ‘had need to boast’, ‘þorfte’ being the past of ‘þurfan’ (‘need’) with an infinitive, and the negative ‘nealles’ reverses it, so the sense is ‘he had no occasion to boast’: his men had given him nothing to boast about. ‘Fyrdgesteallum’ is ‘war-companions’ (‘fyrd’ ‘army’ + ‘gesteall’ ‘companion’), a dative plural after ‘gylpan’. ‘Folccyning’ is ‘folk-king’, Beowulf.

sentences.t:
hwæðre him God ūðe,
sigora Waldend, þæt hē hyne sylfne gewræc
āna mid ecge, þā him wæs elnes þearf.
sentences.l: yet to him God, the Wielder of victories, granted that he avenged himself alone with the edge, when to him there was need of courage.
sentences.i: Yet God, the Wielder of victories, granted him that he should avenge himself alone with his blade, when he had need of courage.
sentences.n: ‘Hwæðre’ is ‘yet, nevertheless’. ‘Him God ūðe’ is ‘God granted him’ (‘ūðe’, past of ‘unnan’, ‘grant’, which takes a dative of the person and a ‘þæt’-clause for the thing granted); ‘sigora Waldend’ is ‘Wielder of victories’ (‘sigor’ ‘victory’ in the genitive plural, ‘Waldend’ the house ‘Wielder’), a title of God in apposition to ‘God’. ‘Þæt hē hyne sylfne gewræc’ is ‘that he avenged himself’ (‘wrecan’ with a reflexive object): he took vengeance for his own death. ‘Āna mid ecge’ is ‘alone with the edge’, the sword, and ‘þā him wæs elnes þearf’ is ‘when to him was need of courage’. The speech turns here from the cowards to what Beowulf did and what Wīglāf did.

sentences.l: I could give him little life-protection at the battle, and began nevertheless beyond my measure to help the kinsman;
sentences.i: I could give him little protection for his life in the fight, and yet I set about helping my kinsman beyond what my strength was fit for;
sentences.n: ‘Ic him līfwraðe lȳtle meahte ætgifan’ is ‘I could little give him life-protection’: ‘līfwraðe’ (‘līf’ ‘life’ + ‘wrāþu’ ‘support, protection’) is the object, ‘ætgifan’ an infinitive (‘give’), ‘him’ the dative, and ‘lȳtle’ ‘little’ as an adverb. Klaeber’s apparatus notes that ‘gifan’ (without ‘æt’) is perhaps the reading. ‘Ond ongan swā þēah’ is ‘and began nevertheless’; ‘ofer mīn gemet’ is ‘beyond my measure’, more than I was fitted for; ‘mǣges helpan’ is ‘help the kinsman’, with ‘helpan’ taking the genitive here (it also takes the dative). Wīglāf is a kinsman of Beowulf, as the poem has said (he is a Wǣgmunding).

sentences.t:
symle wæs þȳ sǣmra, þonne ic sweorde drep
ferhðgenīðlan, fȳr unswīðor
wēoll of gewitte.
sentences.l: Always it was the weaker by that, when I struck with the sword the life-enemy, the fire welled less strongly from his wit.
sentences.i: Each time I struck the deadly foe with my sword, he was the worse for it, and the fire welled less fiercely from his head.
sentences.n: ‘Symle wæs þȳ sǣmra’ is ‘always it was the weaker by that’, ‘þȳ’ an instrumental (‘by that’), ‘sǣmra’ a comparative (‘weaker, worse’) and ‘it’ the dragon, the thing struck. ‘Ferhðgenīðlan’ is ‘life-enemy’ (‘ferhð’ ‘life’ + ‘genīðla’ ‘foe’), accusative, the object of ‘drep’ (past of ‘drepan’, ‘strike’). Sievers and Holthausen read ‘þone’ for ‘þonne’ and ‘-genīðla’, which would make ‘the life-enemy whom I struck’ a noun at the head of the next clause. ‘Fȳr unswīðor wēoll’ is ‘fire less strongly welled’: the manuscript has ‘fyrun (the u altered from an a) swiðor’, Thorpe read ‘fȳr ran swīðor’ (‘fire ran more strongly’), and Rieger and four others ‘fȳr unswīðor’, which Klaeber takes. ‘Of gewitte’ is ‘out of the wit’; I take ‘gewitt’ (‘mind, understanding’) to be the head, the seat of wit, and that is a guess, since the usual sense gives no place for fire to come from.

sentences.t:
Wergendra tō lȳt
þrong ymbe þēoden, þā hyne sīo þrāg becwōm.
sentences.l: Of defenders too few thronged about the prince, when the time of stress came upon him.
sentences.i: Too few defenders pressed about their prince when the time of trial overtook him.
sentences.n: ‘Wergendra’ is a genitive plural, ‘of defenders’, partitive after ‘tō lȳt’ (‘too few’); ‘þrong’ is the past of ‘þringan’ (‘press, throng’) and ‘ymbe þēoden’ is ‘around the prince’. The ‘W’ of ‘Wergendra’ is in italic: the manuscript has ‘fergendra’, which has no meaning, and Grundtvig changed it to ‘wergendra’ (‘defenders’, from ‘werian’, ‘defend’). ‘Sīo þrāg’ is ‘the time (of trouble)’; ‘þrāg’ is ‘a while, a time’ and, as here, a time of stress or distress, and ‘becwōm’ is ‘came upon’ (‘becuman’) with ‘hyne’ as its object. Wīglāf sets his own few against the ten who stayed away.

sentences.l: Now shall treasure-receiving and sword-giving, all native-joy, for your kin, love lie down;
sentences.i: Now the receiving of treasure and the giving of swords, all the joy of the homeland, and all that is dear, shall fail your kin;
sentences.n: ‘Sceal’ is ‘shall, must’, and its subjects are ‘sincþego’ (‘treasure-receiving’, ‘sinc’ ‘treasure’ + ‘þegu’ ‘taking’), ‘swyrdgifu’ (‘sword-gift’) and ‘ēðelwyn’ (‘native-joy’, ‘ēðel’ ‘homeland’ + ‘wynn’ ‘joy’); ‘ēowrum cynne’ is ‘for your kin’, a dative. The verb is ‘ālicgean’ (‘ālicgan’, ‘lie down, fail, cease’). ‘Lufen’ is a puzzle: Klaeber prints ‘lufen’ and I take it as ‘love’ (‘lufu’), but Grimm, Kemble and Trautmann read ‘leofen’ (‘sustenance’), Thorpe ‘lēofum’ and Sedgefield ‘lungre’ (‘quickly’), so it is a guess; ‘i’ gives ‘all that is dear’ for it. The ‘N’ of ‘Nū’ is in italic: the manuscript has ‘hu’, which Grundtvig and Chambers took as exclamatory ‘Hū’ (‘how shall … fail!’), and Kemble and the other editors changed to ‘Nū’, ‘now’. The sense is that the king’s gifts, which the men have had, will end for their whole line.

sentences.t:
londrihtes mōt
þǣre mǣgburge monna ǣghwylc
īdel hweorfan, syððan æðelingas
feorran gefricgean flēam ēowerne,
dōmlēasan dǣd.
sentences.l: Of land-right must each of men of that kin-stronghold go about empty, after nobles from far learn of your flight, the glory-less deed.
sentences.i: Every man of that kindred must go about stripped of his land-right, when nobles far away hear of your flight, that deed without glory.
sentences.n: ‘Londrihtes … īdel hweorfan’ is ‘go about empty of land-right’: ‘īdel’ (‘empty, idle’) takes the genitive, so they will have no right to their land. ‘Monna ǣghwylc þǣre mǣgburge’ is ‘each of men of that kin-stronghold’ (‘mǣg’ ‘kinsman’ + ‘burg’ ‘fortress’), meaning each man of that family. ‘Mōt’ is ‘may, must’; it is bitter here, as in ‘may go about empty’, and I give ‘must’ in both ‘l’ and ‘i’. ‘Syððan æðelingas feorran gefricgean flēam ēowerne’ is ‘after nobles from afar hear of your flight’ (‘gefricgean’ subjunctive, ‘learn by asking’, a long way of saying ‘hear’), and ‘dōmlēasan dǣd’ (‘the glory-less deed’, ‘dōm’ ‘glory’ + ‘-lēas’) stands in apposition to ‘flēam’, accusative. The exile that follows a lord’s shame is real: a man without a lord had no land.

sentences.t:
Dēað bið sēlla
eorla gehwylcum þonne edwītlīf!’
sentences.l: Death is better for each of earls than reproach-life!’
sentences.i: Death is better for any warrior than to live on in reproach!’
sentences.n: ‘Sēlla’ is the comparative ‘better’, and ‘þonne’ is ‘than’, so ‘death is better for each of earls than …’. ‘Edwītlīf’ is ‘reproach-life’ (‘edwīt’ ‘reproach, scorn’ + ‘līf’ ‘life’), a life under shame. The quotation mark closes the speech; the dash and colon that opened it are at 2863. With this Wīglāf puts the choice to the ten: to die with the lord, or to live on under the reproach.
